items.title: Section: If Cessation Were Genuinely Real, Either Everything Would Vanish at Once or Nothing Could Ever Stay Gone — Closing the Debate and Impermanence Itself

items.zh: 謂若滅法別有自性，是實成就；即應此滅有生有滅。若滅生時，一切諸行皆應同滅。如是即應少用功力，如入滅定，諸心心所一切皆滅。若滅滅時，一切諸行雖皆已滅，復應還生，以滅無故。是故言滅有生有滅，不應道理。又善男子、或善女人，於一切時恒有實物自性成就，觀為假有，而能修厭、離欲、解脫，不應道理。與此相違，是應道理。由此行相，是諸菩薩如實了知一切諸行皆是無常。
items.en: If cessation possessed a separate nature of its own, genuinely existing as a real thing, then this very cessation would itself need to have its own arising and its own further cessation. Were this cessation to arise, then every conditioned activity everywhere would have to cease at exactly the same time — meaning it would take only minimal effort, as though simply entering cessation-attainment, for every mental factor whatsoever to cease all at once. Were this cessation itself, having arisen, to then cease, then every conditioned activity, though already extinguished, would have to arise once again, since the cessation that had extinguished them would then itself be absent. This is why saying that cessation has its own arising and its own cessation is unreasonable. Furthermore, it would be unreasonable for a good son or good daughter, if arising, abiding, ageing, and cessation were permanently, genuinely existing real substances at all times, to regard them as merely provisionally existing and thereby be capable of cultivating renunciation, freedom from craving, and liberation; the opposite position is the reasonable one. Through this manner of reasoning, bodhisattvas correctly and thoroughly know that all conditioned activities are impermanent.

items.title: Section: Suffering Opens and Closes — the Classical Three Sufferings Underlying Every Conditioned Activity Without Exception

items.zh: 又諸菩薩，觀無常行相續轉時，能為三種苦所依止。一者、行苦，二者、壞苦，三者、苦苦。如是菩薩如實了知一切諸行皆悉是苦。
items.en: Furthermore, bodhisattvas, observing impermanent activities continuing on in succession, find they serve as the basis for three kinds of suffering: first, conditioning-suffering; second, suffering of reversal; third, suffering of suffering. In this way, bodhisattvas correctly and thoroughly know that all conditioned activities are entirely suffering.

items.title: Section: Non-Self Opens and Closes — No Fixed Person Found Within the Aggregates or Apart From Them, and No Fixed Essence in Any Verbal Label

items.zh: 又諸菩薩，如實了知有為、無為一切諸法二無我性。一者、補特伽羅無我性，二者、法無我性。於諸法中補特伽羅無我性者，謂非即有法，是真實有補特伽羅；亦非離有法，別有真實補特伽羅。於諸法中法無我性者，謂於一切言說事中，一切言說自性諸法都無所有。如是菩薩如實了知一切諸法皆無有我。
items.en: Furthermore, bodhisattvas correctly and thoroughly know the two kinds of selflessness belonging to all phenomena, conditioned and unconditioned alike: first, personal selflessness; second, phenomenal selflessness. Regarding personal selflessness within phenomena: it is not the case that an existing phenomenon is itself a genuinely real person, nor is it the case that, apart from existing phenomena, some further, separately real person exists. Regarding phenomenal selflessness within phenomena: within everything that verbal statement points to, the essence that verbal statement itself attributes simply does not exist at all. In this way, bodhisattvas correctly and thoroughly know that all phenomena are without self.

items.title: Section: Nirvāṇa as Peace Opens — What the Noble Ones Actually Realise, and What Ordinary Bodhisattvas and Śrāvakas Merely Grasp Through Conviction

items.zh: 又諸菩薩，觀一切行先因永斷，後無餘滅，其餘畢竟不起不生，說名涅槃。當知涅槃其體寂靜，一切眾苦畢竟息故，一切煩惱究竟滅故。如是未得清淨增上意樂菩薩，未見聖諦諸聲聞乘，雖於涅槃發起勝解，如是說言涅槃寂靜；而於涅槃未如實解，未能如實正智見轉，然彼亦有如理作意。
items.en: Furthermore, bodhisattvas observe that once the prior cause of every conditioned activity has been permanently severed, and afterwards what remains ceases without remainder, nothing further ever arising again at all — this is called nirvāṇa. One should understand that nirvāṇa's own nature is peace, since every form of suffering is thereby definitively put to rest, and every affliction is thereby completely extinguished. Bodhisattvas who have not yet attained the ground of genuinely pure, excellent aspiration, and śrāvaka practitioners who have not yet directly seen the noble truths, though they raise a genuine conviction regarding nirvāṇa and correctly speak of nirvāṇa as peace, have not yet genuinely understood nirvāṇa, and correct noble wisdom's own direct vision has not yet turned towards it — yet they do already possess correct, reasoned reflection on the matter.

items.title: Section: The Parable of the Toy Chariots — Three Stages From Mistaking a Toy for the Real Thing to Finally Seeing the Genuine Animal Face to Face

items.zh: 譬如王子、或長者子，生育已來，未出王宮、長者內室；王及長者，各為幼童假作種種諸戲樂具，鹿車、牛車、馬車、象車而賜與之。爾時王子及長者子，用為嬉戲，歡娛遊佚，即於如是假所造作鹿、牛、馬、象，發起真實鹿想、牛想、馬想、象想。後於一時，王及長者各知其子漸已長大，諸根成熟，讚說真實鹿、牛、馬、象。爾時王子及長者子聞父讚說，作是念言：今者父王及父長者，將非讚說我等所有鹿、牛、馬、象四種車耶？復於後時，王及長者知子轉大，從內宮室引出外遊，示其真實鹿、牛、馬、象。時彼見已，內自發生如實慧解，此為實義鹿車、牛車、馬車、象車。父於長夜甞為我等讚說斯事，然唯我等以無智故，於不如實唯彼相似、唯彼影像發起真實鹿等勝解。由是因緣，於先勝解追起羞愧。
items.en: Suppose a prince or a wealthy merchant's son, from the time of birth, has never yet left the royal palace or the merchant's own inner chambers. The king and the merchant each fashion, for their young children, various playthings shaped like a deer, an ox, a horse, and an elephant, and give these to them. The prince and the merchant's son, playing joyfully and delightedly with these toys, thereby give rise to a genuine notion of deer, of ox, of horse, and of elephant regarding these merely fabricated objects. Later, at a certain time, the king and the merchant, each recognising that their child has gradually grown and whose faculties have matured, praise and describe the genuine deer, ox, horse, and elephant. Hearing their fathers' praise, the prince and the merchant's son think to themselves: "Could it be that what our father the king and our father the merchant now praise is not exactly these four kinds of chariot we already possess?" Later still, once the king and the merchant recognise their children have grown further, they lead them out from the inner palace to travel abroad, and show them the genuine deer, ox, horse, and elephant. Upon seeing these, genuine, realised understanding spontaneously dawns within them: these are the true deer-chariot, ox-chariot, horse-chariot, and elephant-chariot in their real sense. Our father has, across this long night of time, always praised and described this very thing to us, yet we, lacking genuine wisdom, gave rise, towards what was not genuinely real but merely resembled it, merely its own reflection, to the conviction that it was the genuine deer and the rest. Because of this, they feel genuine shame recalling their former conviction.

items.title: Section: Mapping the Parable — the Palace as Saṃsāra, the Father as the Buddha, and the Toy Chariot as Nirvāṇa's Own Rough, Preliminary Sketch

items.zh: 如是宮室，喻於生死。其所生育諸幼童子，喻未證得清淨增上意樂菩薩，及未見諦諸聲聞乘。父喻諸佛及已證入大地菩薩。先為假作鹿、牛等車，喻為宣說涅槃鹿相。次為讚說真實鹿等，喻佛菩薩自現證見真實涅槃，如其所見，於彼菩薩及聲聞前，讚說涅槃真實功德。所餘，喻彼既聞是已，但用隨順音聲覺慧，於涅槃德長夜勝解。若於是時資糧成熟，漸次增長，成淨增上意樂菩薩、見諦聲聞，於真涅槃生現證智；即於爾時發生自內如實慧解，如是涅槃，一切聲聞、獨覺所證，諸佛菩薩先所讚說，我等先以愚夫覺慧，於不如實唯彼相似、唯彼影像發起真實涅槃勝解。由是因緣，於先勝解追生羞愧。依止於後如實勝解。
items.en: The inner palace represents saṃsāra. The young children raised there represent bodhisattvas who have not yet attained genuinely pure, excellent aspiration, and śrāvaka practitioners who have not yet directly seen the noble truths. The father represents both the buddhas and bodhisattvas who have already attained the great grounds. The fabricated deer-chariot and the rest, given at first, represent teaching nirvāṇa's own rough characteristics through language. Praising the genuine deer and the rest afterwards represents buddhas and bodhisattvas, having directly realised and seen true nirvāṇa themselves, describing, exactly as they themselves have seen it, the genuine merit of nirvāṇa before those bodhisattvas and śrāvakas. The rest represents those who, having heard this, come only to a conviction, sustained across a long night, regarding nirvāṇa's own merit, based merely on following the sound of what was spoken. Should the provisions of the path, at some point, mature and gradually increase, so that one becomes a bodhisattva of pure, excellent aspiration or a śrāvaka who has directly seen the truths, giving rise to directly realised wisdom regarding true nirvāṇa — at that very time, genuinely realised understanding spontaneously arises from within: this very nirvāṇa is exactly what every śrāvaka and solitary realiser has attained, exactly what buddhas and bodhisattvas had already praised beforehand, while we ourselves, previously possessing only an unenlightened being's own understanding, had given rise, towards what was not genuinely real but merely resembled it, merely its own reflection, to the conviction that we had already attained genuine nirvāṇa. Because of this, genuine shame arises in recalling that earlier conviction, now resting instead on this later, genuinely realised conviction.

blocks.text: The remaining three seals, and a parable about toy carts showing how far ordinary understanding of nirvāṇa is from the real thing.

"If cessation arose, all conditioned activities would cease together; with minimal effort, as if entering cessation-attainment, all mind and mental factors would end." Venerable Miào Jìng: if cessation were that powerful, practitioners would not need to practise at all.

The three kinds of suffering underlie every conditioned activity. Master Cháng Bǎi: the suffering of conditioning is the ultimate suffering, hard for ordinary people to understand; among feelings it is the neutral one. Venerable Miào Jìng: even deep meditative states fall within it.

"No existing phenomenon is itself a genuinely real person, nor, apart from existing phenomena, is there some separately real person." Master Cháng Bǎi: no self in the formations, none apart from them.

Venerable Miào Jìng: "the prior cause permanently cut" is nirvāṇa with remainder; "afterwards ceasing without remainder" is nirvāṇa without remainder; concentration without wisdom gives only a temporary peace. Only noble ones realise it; bodhisattvas below the first ground and śrāvaka disciples grasp it only by conviction. Venerable Miào Jìng: a little stillness in calming practice is not the real thing.

Venerable Miào Jìng: the prince stands for Mahāyāna Buddhists, the merchant's son for Hīnayāna Buddhists; the four carts stand for four kinds of nirvāṇa. Master Cháng Bǎi: the prince's father is the Buddha as bodhisattvas see him, the merchant is the Buddha as śrāvakas see him.
The treatise explains each part of the story: what we imagine nirvāṇa to be is like a toy cart beside the real one.
The parable is humbling. Whatever we picture when we hear "nirvāṇa" is a toy. That is not a reason to stop; it is a reason to keep practising until we see the real thing.

quiz.q: If cessation were a real thing, what would happen when it arose?
options: all formations would cease at once — with little effort, like entering cessation, all mind and mental factors would end
quiz.why: "If cessation arose, all conditioned activities would cease together — with minimal effort, as if entering cessation-attainment, all mind and mental factors would end." Venerable Miào Jìng: if cessation were that powerful, practitioners needn't practice at all.

quiz.q: Of the three sufferings, how do the lectures explain conditioning-suffering?
options: Cháng Bǎi: the ultimate suffering — the neutral feeling; Miào Jìng: even deep meditative states fall under it
quiz.why: Master Cháng Bǎi: conditioning-suffering is the ultimate suffering, hard for ordinary people to understand — among feelings, the neutral one. Venerable Miào Jìng: even deep meditative states fall within it.

quiz.q: How does the treatise define personal selflessness?
options: no existing phenomenon is a real person, nor is there a real person apart from them
quiz.why: "No existing phenomenon is itself a genuinely real person, nor, apart from existing phenomena, is there some separately real person." Master Cháng Bǎi: no self in the formations, none apart from them. Venerable Miào Jìng: no self apart from the body, none in the body.

quiz.q: "The prior cause permanently cut, afterwards ceasing without remainder" — the English is muddled. How does Venerable Miào Jìng read it?
options: the prior cause cut is nirvāṇa with remainder; ceasing without remainder is nirvāṇa without remainder
quiz.why: Venerable Miào Jìng: "the prior cause permanently cut" is nirvāṇa with remainder; "afterwards ceasing without remainder" is nirvāṇa without remainder; concentration without wisdom is only temporary. The English phrasing obscures this.

quiz.q: Bodhisattvas "not yet with pure excellent aspiration" speak of nirvāṇa's peace without real understanding. Who has pure excellent aspiration, according to Venerable Miào Jìng?
quiz.why: Venerable Miào Jìng: bodhisattvas of pure excellent aspiration are those of the first ground, Joy; a little stillness in calming practice is not the real thing. Master Cháng Bǎi: those lacking it are ordinary bodhisattvas and śrāvaka disciples.

quiz.q: In the toy-chariot parable, how do the lectures map the prince and the merchant's son?
options: both: the prince is the Buddha

Miào Jìng: the prince is Mahāyāna, the merchant's son Hīnayāna, the four carts four nirvāṇas; Cháng Bǎi: the prince's father is the Buddha as bodhisattvas see him, the merchant the Buddha as śrāvakas see him
quiz.why: Venerable Miào Jìng: the prince stands for Mahāyāna Buddhists, the merchant's son for Hīnayāna Buddhists; the four carts stand for four kinds of nirvāṇa. Master Cháng Bǎi: the prince's father is the Buddha as seen by bodhisattvas, the merchant the Buddha as seen by śrāvakas.
